title: Introduction to R
text:
R programming language
R first appeared in 1993 and is a programming language designed for working with data and statistics.
R is usually interpreted: you write commands and R runs them directly, without a separate compile step.
For example, ask R to do a calculation:

2 + 2

[1] 4

title: Introduction to R
text:
Functions in R
You can define functions in R like:

sumFun <- function(a, b) {
  a + b
}

And use them later as:

sumFun(5, 6)

[1] 11

title: Introduction to R
text:
Packages in R
Packages are collections of functions and other tools that people develop and share for you to use.
Many R packages are distributed through CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network), a collection of servers that hosts R packages and checks submitted updates. Package authors maintain their packages; CRAN helps make them available to the R community.

To install a package you can just type:

install.packages("tibble")
# or, if you have pak installed
pak::pkg_install("tibble")



You can either call a function using :::

tibble::tibble(a = 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <dbl>
1     1




Or using library(), which makes the package’s functions available:

library(tibble)
tibble(a = 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <dbl>
1     1




In general we will use the latter option (library()).

title: Introduction to R
text:
The pipe operator |>

The pipe operator was introduced in R 4.1 and it is widely used in R. It concatenates the use of two functions, for example:

library(dplyr)

x <- tibble(a = 1)
x

# A tibble: 1 × 1
      a
  <dbl>
1     1

x <- mutate(x, b = 1)
x

# A tibble: 1 × 2
      a     b
  <dbl> <dbl>
1     1     1



You can simplify this code with:

x <- tibble(a = 1) |>
  mutate(b = 1)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Meet the tidyverse
The tidyverse is a collection of R packages that work well together for common data tasks.


dplyr: wrangle data (filter, select, create columns, summarise)

ggplot2: make plots

readr and tidyr: read and reshape data
plus packages for strings, factors, iteration, and more

title: Introduction to R
section: Some examples: a consistent way to work with data
text:
Some examples: a consistent way to work with data
Tidyverse functions use a consistent style: give a data frame to a function, and get a data frame back.

library(tibble)

people <- tibble(
  name = c("Alex", "Sam", "Jo"),
  age = c(24, 31, 19),
  group = c("A", "B", "A")
)

people

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  name    age group
  <chr> <dbl> <chr>
1 Alex     24 A    
2 Sam      31 B    
3 Jo       19 A    


tibble() is the tidyverse’s friendly take on a data frame. It prints a quick preview and keeps the data in a familiar rectangular format.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Read, transform, and summarise
Use |> to read a data workflow from top to bottom. Here we keep adults, add a column, and count people in each group:

library(dplyr)
people |>
  filter(age >= 18) |>
  mutate(age_next_year = age + 1) |>
  count(group)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  group     n
  <chr> <int>
1 A         2
2 B         1



Some handy dplyr verbs:


filter() keeps rows

select() keeps columns

mutate() creates or changes columns

summarise() calculates a summary

arrange() sorts rows

title: Introduction to R
text:
What is an R Project?
An R Project is a folder for one piece of work, with a small .Rproj file that lets RStudio recognise and reopen it.

Keep your scripts, notes, data, and results together
RStudio opens the project folder as the working directory
Use paths relative to the project, so your code is easier to share and rerun

Think of it as a tidy home for an analysis. One project per workshop or analysis is a good place to start.

title: Introduction to R
text:
A simple project layout
There is no single right layout. Start small and add folders when you need them:
my-analysis/
├── my-analysis.Rproj
├── R/                 # scripts and functions
├── data/              # input data (keep originals unchanged)
└── Results/           # tables, plots, and other outputs
RStudio creates the .Rproj file for you. You create the folders that make sense for your work.

title: Introduction to R
section: Let’s create your first R Project
text:
Let’s create your first R Project
In RStudio:

Choose File → New Project…

Choose New Directory, then New Project

Give it a name, for example r-introduction, and choose where to save it
Select Create Project


You should now see the project name in the top-right of RStudio. Save this presentation’s practice script inside the project, then make folders such as data and Results if you need them.

title: Introduction to R
section: Find the project root with here
text:
Find the project root with here


library(here)
here()

[1] "/home/runner/work/HDS-OMOP-course/HDS-OMOP-course"




dir.create(here("Results"))

That creates a Results folder in the project root. You can use the same idea to read or save files inside the project.

We should always work within an R Project for each analysis.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
CodelistGenerator

The CodelistGenerator R package provides tools to


Explore OMOP CDM vocabularies available in the database
Generate codelists systematically using vocabulary-based search strategies
Generate codelist diagnostics to assess code use and identify potentially missing concepts

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Generating candidate concepts
Today, we’ll focus on the getCandidateCodes() function to identify candidate concepts for our two phenotypes.

getCandidateCodes(
  cdm,
  keywords,
  exclude = NULL,
  domains = "Condition",
  vocabularyId = NULL,
  standardConcept = "Standard",
  searchInSynonyms = FALSE,
  searchNonStandard = FALSE,
  includeDescendants = TRUE,
  includeAncestor = FALSE
)


The function returns candidate concepts for review, together with the search strategy used to identify them.
This allows us to define a systematic and reproducible codelist search strategy.

Note


A refined search strategy does not mean we have a final codelist.

Before cohort construction, this preliminary codelist is clinically reviewed.
Once cohorts are created, diagnostics provide further evidence to support additional codelist review and refinement.

CohortConstructor

CohortConstructor provides tools to create and manipulate cohorts using the OMOP CDM.

Create base cohorts from codelists
Apply demographic and observation requirements

Apply additional clinical requirements

Define cohort entry and exit


Combine, collapse, and manipulate cohort records

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Primary hypertension cohort

We will progressively apply our cohort inclusion criteria to identify adults with primary (essential) hypertension.

Create a base cohort from our essential hypertension codelist
Require ≥ 180 days of prior observation

Restrict to age ≥ 18 years

Require a second hypertension record within 365 days

Exit at end of observation

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Primary hypertension cohort
→ Create the base cohort
We first create a base cohort from condition records corresponding to concepts in our preliminary hypertension codelist:

hypertensionCodelist <- list("essential_hypertension" = hypertensionCodes$concept_id)

cdm$essential_hypertension_base <- conceptCohort(
  cdm = cdm,
  conceptSet = hypertensionCodelist,
  name = "essential_hypertension_base"
)


At this stage, each qualifying hypertension record can contribute to cohort entry.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Primary hypertension cohort
→ Apply the inclusion criteria
Now we apply inclusion criteria in a pipeline-fashion to refine the base cohort:

cdm$essential_hypertension <- cdm$essential_hypertension_base |>

  # Age ≥18 and ≥180 days of prior observation
  requireDemographics(
    ageRange = c(18, 150),
    minPriorObservation = 180,
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  ) |>

  # Require another hypertension record within 365 days
  requireCohortIntersect(
    targetCohortTable = "essential_hypertension_base",
    window = c(1, 365),
    intersections = c(1, Inf),
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  ) |>

  # Follow until the end of observation
  exitAtObservationEnd(
    name = "essential_hypertension"
  )

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
More complex phenotype definitions
Our primary hypertension cohort was a simple example to illustrate the workflow.
We can also implement more complex phenotype definitions combining different types of clinical evidence.

For instance we could use systolic and diastolic blood pressure measurements:

cdm$systolic_blood_pressure <- measurementCohort(
  cdm = cdm, 
  conceptSet = codelist["systolic_blood_pressure"],
  valueAsNumber = list(c(140, 99999)),
  name = "systolic_blood_pressure"
)

cdm$diastolic_blood_pressure <- measurementCohort(
  cdm = cdm, 
  conceptSet = codelist["diastolic_blood_pressure"],
  valueAsNumber = list(c(90, 99999)),
  name = "diastolic_blood_pressure"
)

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Warfarin cohort
→ Create treatment episodes and identify new users
We now combine nearby exposures into treatment episodes and apply our new-user criteria:

cdm$warfarin_new_users <- cdm$warfarin_base |>

  # Collapse exposures separated by ≤30 days
  collapseCohorts(
    gap = 30,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # Require ≥365 days of prior observation
  requireDemographics(
    minPriorObservation = 365,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # No warfarin exposure during the previous 365 days
  requireCohortIntersect(
    targetCohortTable = "warfarin_base",
    window = c(-365, -1),
    intersections = 0,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  )

text:
PhenotypeR
PhenotypeR provides a standardised set of diagnostics to review and evaluate phenotypes created using the OMOP CDM.







Database diagnostics

databaseDiagnostics()








Codelist diagnostics

codelistDiagnostics()






Cohort diagnostics

cohortDiagnostics()








Population diagnostics

populationDiagnostics()

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Database Diagnostics
Summarise the database metadata including:

Snapshot
Summary of the person table

Summary of the observation period

Summary of the clinical tables (e.g., condition_occurrence) where concepts from the codelists defining the cohorts are found.









Note








Database diagnostics use functionality from OmopSketch.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Codelist Diagnostics

Summarise the codelist associated with your cohort including:


Achilles codes use (only if ACHILLES tables are present)

Orphan codes use (only if ACHILLES tables are present)
Cohort code use

Measurement code use (only if measurement concepts are present in your codelist)

Drug diagnostics (only if drug concepts are present in your codelist)










Note








Codelist diagnostics use functionality from CodelistGenerator to evaluate the use of concepts from our codelists in the OMOP CDM.
If the codelists contain measurement concepts, MeasurementDiagnostics is used to evaluate those concepts.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text: Cohort Diagnostics

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Cohort Diagnostics
Summarise and evaluate the cohorts including:

Cohort count & attrition

Cohort characteristics — Baseline characteristics of the cohort

Large-scale characteristics — Clinical records observed in different time windows

Compare cohorts — Overlap and timing between cohorts (if multiple cohorts)


Cohort survival — Survival until death (if death table is available)










Note








Cohort diagnostics use functionality from CohortCharacteristics to characterise and compare cohorts, and CohortSurvival to perform survival analyses.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Population Diagnostics

Contextualises the frequency of your study cohorts in the database calculating:

Incidence
Period Prevalence










Note








Population diagnostics use functionality from IncidencePrevalence to estimate the incidence and prevalence of our cohorts in the database population.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Run diagnostics together
Rather than running each diagnostic separately, phenotypeDiagnostics() allows us to run them together.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cohort,
  databaseDiagnostics = list(),
  codelistDiagnostics = list(),
  cohortDiagnostics = list(),
  populationDiagnostics = list()
)


We can choose which diagnostics to run and customise their parameters.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cohort,
  databaseDiagnostics = list(),
  codelistDiagnostics = list(),
  cohortDiagnostics = list(
    cohortSample = 1000
  ),
  populationDiagnostics = NULL
)

section: Run diagnostics of hypertension and warfarin cohorts together
text:
Run diagnostics of hypertension and warfarin cohorts together
We created our two cohort separately. To run phenotyper, we can bring them together into a single cohort table and then run PhenotypeR functions to this table.

cdm <- bind(
  cdm$essential_hypertension,
  cdm$warfarin_new_users,
  name = "phenotypes"
)
cdm$phenotypes |> settings()

Run phenotype diagnostics

Now we can evaluate both phenotypes using the same standardised diagnostic workflow.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(cohort = cdm$phenotypes)



Then we can use the function shinyDiagnostics to create a shinyApp to review results:



shinyDiagnostics(result = result, directory = here())

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
section: Git vs GitHub vs GitHub Desktop
text:
Git vs GitHub vs GitHub Desktop

Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in source code during software development and allows multiple developers to collaborate efficiently.


GitHub is a web-based platform that provides hosting for Git repositories, along with collaborative features like issue tracking, pull requests, and project management.


GitHub Desktop is a graphical user interface (GUI) application that simplifies the interaction with Git and GitHub, allowing users to perform common repository operations without using the command line.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Repository (Repo)
A repository is essentially a project’s folder. It contains all the project files, including code, documentation, images, and, most importantly, the entire history of every change made to those files.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Explore repository
https://github.com/oxford-pharmacoepi/Tidy-R-programming-with-OMOP

A README.md is a useful front page for a repository. It can include:

A summary of the repository.
Instructions for installing a package, running code, or using a tool.
An overview of the repository folders.
How to contribute.
License information.
Acknowledgments.
Contact details.
Citation information.

# to add a heading.

Commit
A commit is a snapshot of your repository at a specific point in time. Commits are the building blocks of Git history.

Every commit has a unique ID (SHA), an author, a timestamp, and a commit message that explains why the change was made.
Commits are created locally with Git.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Push & Pull
These are the actions used to synchronise your local Git repository with the remote repository on GitHub:

Push: Send your committed changes from your computer to the remote repository on GitHub.
Pull: Fetch changes from GitHub and integrate them into your current local branch. We will practise this later.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Issues

An issue is a place to track a task, bug, or idea. It gives the team a place to discuss the work, assign responsibility, and keep track of progress.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Issues

Labels: Labels are tags used to categorise and organise issues by topic, priority, or status.
Assignee: The assignee is the person responsible for handling or resolving the issue.
Type: The type describes the issue, for example a bug, feature request, or task.

Check your GitHub inbox for the request to review a colleague’s codelist. Open the request and follow the link to the issue or pull request.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Clone
Clone a repository to make a local copy on your computer. To make a copy in your GitHub account, fork the repository.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Branch
A branch is an independent line of development.

The default and main line of development is typically called the main branch.
Branches allow developers to work on new features or bug fixes in isolation without affecting the stable, main code.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Fork
A fork is a copy of a repository in your GitHub account. You can change your fork without changing the original, then propose your changes to the original project with a pull request. A fork is useful when you do not have write access to the original repository.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Pull Request (PR)
A pull request (PR) proposes changes from one branch to another, usually so the team can discuss and review them before merging.

PRs are where discussion, code review, and automated testing happen before the code is integrated.

A merge integrates changes from one branch into another. Once a pull request is approved, a repository maintainer can merge it into the target branch.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
.gitignore

The .gitignore file tells git which files or folders to skip when tracking changes. It prevents temporary, sensitive, or unnecessary files from being added to a repository. Common examples include log files, build artifacts, and environment files. This keeps the repo clean and focused on essential code and assets.

To ignore a file, add its name, for example my_file.txt.
To ignore a folder, add its name followed by a slash, for example folder/.
Use patterns such as *.txt to ignore all .txt files.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
text:
Merge conflicts
A merge conflict happens when Git cannot automatically combine overlapping changes. Conflicts can be resolved; they are a normal part of working together.

Keep pull requests focused and reasonably small.
Update your branch from main regularly, especially before opening a pull request.
If GitHub Desktop reports a conflict, review the conflicting changes and ask for help if you are unsure how to resolve them.

title: GitHub and GitHub Desktop
section: Link a pull request to an issue
text:
Link a pull request to an issue
To link an issue and close it when the pull request is merged into the repository’s default branch, put one of these keywords followed by the issue number in the pull request description:

close #12 / closes #12
resolve #12 / resolves #12
fix #12 / fixes #12


To link an issue without using a closing keyword, link it manually from the Development section of the pull request sidebar.
